# Exercise 8

## Correlation

Compute the correlation coefficient between any two variables.
```{r correlation}
    # Compute the correlation coefficient between Duration and Commision
    correlation <- cor(travel_insurance$Duration, travel_insurance$Commisioninvalue)
    correlation
```

Compute the Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall correlations between any two variables.
```{r correlations}
    # Compute Pearson correlation
    pearson_corr <- cor(travel_insurance$Duration, travel_insurance$Commisioninvalue, method = "pearson")
    # Compute Spearman correlation
    spearman_corr <- cor(travel_insurance$Duration, travel_insurance$Commisioninvalue, method = "spearman")
    # Compute Kendall correlation
    kendall_corr <- cor(travel_insurance$Duration, travel_insurance$Commisioninvalue, method = "kendall")
```

Create a correlation matrix for all variables.
```{r correlation_matrix}
    # Select only numeric columns for correlation matrix
    numeric_data <- travel_insurance[sapply(travel_insurance, is.numeric)]
    # Compute the correlation matrix
    correlation_matrix <- cor(numeric_data, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
    correlation_matrix
```

Compute the covariance between any two variables.
```{r covariance}
    # Compute the covariance between Duration and Commission
    covariance <- cov(travel_insurance$Duration, travel_insurance$Commisioninvalue, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
    covariance
```

Compute the Cosine Similarity between the same two variables as you used for #2. Plot the two together.
```{r cosine_similarity}
    # Compute Cosine Similarity
    cosine_similarity <- sum(travel_insurance$Duration * travel_insurance$Commisioninvalue) / 
                         (sqrt(sum(travel_insurance$Duration^2)) * sqrt(sum(travel_insurance$Commisioninvalue^2)))
    cosine_similarity
    # Plot Duration vs Commission
    plot(travel_insurance$Duration, travel_insurance$Commisioninvalue, 
         main = "Duration vs Commission", 
         xlab = "Duration", 
         ylab = "Commission", 
         pch = 19, 
         col = "blue")
```

## Confidence Intervals

Compute the average confidence interval for each numeric feature.
```{r confidence_intervals}
    # Compute confidence intervals for each numeric feature
    confidence_intervals <- sapply(numeric_data, function(x) {
        mean_x <- mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
        sd_x <- sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
        n_x <- sum(!is.na(x))
        error_margin <- qt(0.975, df = n_x - 1) * (sd_x / sqrt(n_x))
        lower_bound <- mean_x - error_margin
        upper_bound <- mean_x + error_margin
        return(c(lower_bound, upper_bound))
    })
    confidence_intervals
```

Compute the t-scores for each numeric feature.
```{r t_scores}
    # Compute t-scores for each numeric feature
    t_scores <- sapply(numeric_data, function(x) {
        mean_x <- mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
        sd_x <- sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
        n_x <- sum(!is.na(x))
        t_score <- (mean_x - 0) / (sd_x / sqrt(n_x))  # Assuming population mean is 0
        return(t_score)
    })
    t_scores
```

What do those values mean logically?

- The confidence intervals provide a range of values within which we can be reasonably confident that the true population mean lies, based on our sample data. A wider interval indicates more uncertainty, while a narrower interval suggests more precision in our estimate.
- The t-scores indicate how many standard deviations the sample mean is from the hypothesized population mean (in this case, 0). A higher absolute t-score suggests that the sample mean is significantly different from the population mean, while a t-score close to 0 indicates that the sample mean is not significantly different from the population mean.
